this adjusted effect represents a 25% relative increase over the baseline red card rate

spans.assertion: the sample contains 1,359 unique players and 2,834 unique referees
the outcome variable was defined as a binary indicator of any red card received in the dyad
1,344 dyads (1.25%) had at least one red card
two independent raters coded player skin tone from photos on a 5-point scale (0.0 very light to 1.0 very dark)
inter-rater reliability was Pearson r=0.923 and Spearman rho=0.858 (both p<.001)
99.9% exact or adjacent-category agreement was found between raters
players with average rating 0.0-0.25 were classified as light skin tone (90,116 dyads, 83.7%)
players with average rating 0.75-1.0 were classified as dark skin tone (17,490 dyads, 16.3%)
middle categories (0.375-0.625) were excluded to obtain a clearer contrast
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded due to missing skin tone data
log(games), the natural log of number of games in the dyad, was included as a covariate as the key exposure control
position (6 categories: Defender, Forward, Goalkeeper, Midfielder, Winger, Unknown) was included as a covariate
league (4 countries: England, France, Germany, Spain) was included as a covariate
games played was included as a covariate because more games means more opportunity for cards
position was included as a covariate to account for differential foul rates by playing role
league was included as a covariate to capture country-specific referee behavior and game culture
height and weight were tested in a sensitivity analysis but excluded from the primary model to maximize sample size, since including them would only lose 686 dyads with negligible impact on results
logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors was used as the statistical method
clustering was done by player, since skin tone is a player-level characteristic
the primary estimand was calculated using Average Marginal Effect (AME)
predicted probabilities were calculated for all dyads under both skin tone conditions
the risk difference was averaged across all observed covariate patterns
AME is asserted to be more robust than conditional predictions at representative values
confidence intervals were computed via cluster bootstrap with 200 iterations, resampling players
dyads with missing skin tone ratings (21,407; 14.7%) were excluded
dyads with middle skin tone ratings 0.375-0.625 (17,015; 11.7%) were excluded
dyads with missing position or league data (<1%) were excluded
the final analysis sample was 107,606 dyads, 73.7% of the original 146,028
games was log-transformed to normalize its right-skewed distribution (range 1-47 games per dyad)
skin tone was dichotomized as described above
cluster-robust standard errors (clustered by player) were used to account for within-player correlation across multiple dyads
no weighting was applied; each dyad was weighted equally
no fixed effects were used; covariate adjustment was done via regression instead
the decision recorded for the hypothesis is SUPPORTED
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players is strongly supported by the data
the adjusted risk difference of +0.290 pp is small in absolute terms but meaningful given the low base rate of red cards (1.25%), representing a 24% relative increase in risk
the 95% CI [0.120, 0.510] excludes zero, indicating a statistically significant effect, with the lower bound representing a non-trivial 10% relative increase
p=0.003, well below alpha=0.05, provides strong evidence against the null hypothesis of no difference
the effect is in the hypothesized direction (dark greater than light) for both primary and secondary estimands
results remain significant after adjusting for key confounders (games, position, league)
a sensitivity analysis including height and weight yields similar results (OR=1.216, p=0.031)
the unadjusted analysis is also significant (p=0.031), though with a slightly smaller effect
both the risk difference (additive scale) and odds ratio (multiplicative scale) show statistically significant effects in the same direction
the unadjusted red card rate for light-skinned players is 1,096/90,116 = 1.22%
the unadjusted red card rate for dark-skinned players is 248/17,490 = 1.42%

the sample composition is 107,606 total dyads, 90,116 (83.7%) light skin, 17,490 (16.3%) dark skin, 1,359 unique players, 2,834 unique referees, and 1,344 red cards (1.25% of dyads)
